title: Forza Horizon 6 -- Up to scratch?
subtitle: Is the long-awaited Horizon game set in Japan going to deliver?
content:
## The Festival Comes to Japan

For years, if you asked any Forza Horizon fan where they wanted the next game to go, the answer was almost always Japan. Mountains with tight hairpin corners, neon-lit city streets, winding touge roads cutting through forests — it was the dream setting. Playground Games finally delivered it on May 19th, 2026, and the result is one of the best racing games I've ever played.

I've put serious hours into FH6 now, and I can say pretty confidently: Japan was worth the wait.

## The Map is Stunning

The open world is the biggest Horizon has ever built. Tokyo alone is five times larger than any previous city in the series, and it shows — you can spend a full evening just cruising through its streets without running the same road twice. But the city is only part of it.

Outside Tokyo you've got mountain passes dusted with snow, rice fields cutting through the lowlands, coastal highways, dense forests, and the unmistakable silhouette of Mt. Fuji looming in the background. Playground didn't try to recreate Japan one-to-one. Instead they described their approach as capturing the *essence* of the place — a smoother, condensed version of the real thing. It works brilliantly. Every biome feels distinct, and driving between them never gets old.

## 550+ Cars and Japanese Car Culture

This is where FH6 really shines for anyone who loves cars beyond just racing. The launch roster sits at over 550 vehicles, and there's a genuine focus on Japanese car culture that previous entries couldn't offer. Kei cars, classic JDM legends, modified street machines — they're all here and they feel right at home on these roads.

The cover cars are the 2025 Toyota GR GT Prototype and the 2025 Toyota Land Cruiser, which tells you everything about the tone Playground was going for. This isn't just a game that happens to be set in Japan — it actually engages with what makes Japanese car culture interesting.

## New Race Types That Actually Change Things

Touge Battles are the headline new addition, and they deliver. Racing bumper-to-bumper down a narrow mountain road, trading paint through tight hairpins at speed, is a completely different feeling from anything in FH5. It's tense, it's chaotic, and it suits the setting perfectly.

Treasure Cars are back too — hidden vehicles scattered across the map that need to be found and restored before you can race them. It's a great excuse to go exploring off the beaten path and stumble across corners of the map you'd never see otherwise.

## Does It Feel Like a Racing Game?

Here's my honest take, and this comes from someone who actually makes racing games: FH6 is still very much an arcade racer. Collisions are forgiving, physics are approachable, and you're never more than a rewind button away from fixing a mistake. If you're coming in hoping for a sim experience, look elsewhere.

But that accessibility is a feature, not a flaw. The Horizon series has always been about the freedom of driving — the feeling of flying down a mountain road in a car you love, with something great on the soundtrack, in a world that looks incredible. FH6 delivers that better than any game before it.

The storyline is thin, as it always has been in Horizon games. You're here for the driving, not the cutscenes. That's fine.

## A Note from Someone Who Makes Racing Games

Working on my own racing game project, I pay close attention to how games like this handle the feel of speed and the design of their tracks. FH6 does something really clever with its road layouts — even in the open world, the roads are subtly shaped to encourage momentum and flow. You're rarely fighting the environment. You're working with it.

The way the touge roads in particular are designed — tight enough to feel dangerous, wide enough to be fair — is something I've been thinking about a lot since playing. It's a masterclass in making the player feel skilled without making the game feel easy.

## Verdict

Forza Horizon 6 is the best game in the series and one of the best racing games ever made. The Japan setting delivers everything fans imagined and then some, the car roster is the strongest yet, and the new race types add genuine variety without feeling gimmicky.

It's not perfect — the story is forgettable and the arcade physics will put off sim fans — but those are small complaints against an enormous, beautiful, endlessly fun package.

**9 / 10** — Japan was worth the 14-year wait.

---

*Forza Horizon 6 is available now on Xbox Series X/S and PC via the Xbox app and Steam. It's included with Game Pass Ultimate at no extra cost.*

title: Welcome to PulseNet
subtitle: Your new home for game dev news, guides, and dev logs. Start writing to make it your own.
content:
## Welcome to PulseNet!

This is your personal game news and dev log site. Here's how to get started:

### Writing Articles

Click the **✦ WRITER** button in the top right and enter your passcode to open the editor.

### Publishing to GitHub Pages

1. Write your articles in the editor
2. Export the `articles.json` file
3. Put it in the same folder as `index.html`
4. Commit and push to your repo

> Your friends will see your articles at your GitHub Pages link automatically.

### Markdown Support

Articles support full Markdown formatting:

- **Bold** and *italic* text
- Headings with ## and ###
- Blockquotes
- Lists
- `Inline code`

---

Have fun building!
